paragraphs: Teaching a language model a specialized skill can damage abilities it already had, even when the update is narrow. ALER addresses this continual-learning problem when the original pretraining data is unavailable. Its central idea is to actively search for behaviors at risk of being forgotten during adaptation.

The method keeps a frozen reference model and searches for a small collection of latent prompt embeddings: internal representations that act as inputs. This search deliberately maximizes disagreement between the adapting model’s output scores and those of the reference. The resulting embeddings expose vulnerable behaviors. ALER then uses online distillation on these inputs to bring the adapting model closer to the reference while continuing target-domain learning.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees concerning the efficiency of this targeted repair. Experiments across two specialized fine-tuning datasets and six general-purpose benchmarks show a consistently better balance between retaining previous abilities and acquiring new ones than the evaluated baselines. The findings support proactive repair as a way to improve that balance without needing access to pretraining examples.
icml-2026-adversarial-latent-embedding-r.tldr: ALER searches for internal inputs that expose forgetting, then distills a frozen model’s behavior to preserve prior abilities during fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Vision-text compression represents textual material visually, allowing dense visual tokens to carry long contexts. The paper identifies a gap between reading this material and reasoning with it: models can decode the words accurately yet struggle with retrieval across long inputs or deductions requiring several steps. Strong reasoning on ordinary text therefore does not automatically transfer to its visually compressed equivalent.

The authors find that standard supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on visual prompts make only limited progress relative to training on text. Their proposed CoRe framework coordinates the two forms of reasoning. It uses the text-conditioned policy as an evolving reference and matches the visual-conditioned policy’s output distributions at successive reasoning steps. This coordination fits into both supervised and reinforcement-learning pipelines.

Across mathematical reasoning, long-context memory, and table retrieval, CoRe substantially improves on standard visual post-training. It recovers up to 70% of the performance gap against the textual upper bound. That result indicates that explicitly coordinating reasoning across modalities can help models use capabilities that ordinary visual post-training struggles to activate.
icml-2026-awakening-visual-reasoning-mit.tldr: CoRe aligns visual reasoning with text-based reasoning during training, recovering up to 70% of the gap caused by visual text compression.

paragraphs: Generating individually convincing images does not ensure that the same subject remains recognizable across a sequence. This paper investigates consistency through the representations of the text prompts themselves. The authors find that these representations already implicitly contain signals associated with subject identity, which they call Identity-Preserving Embeddings.

BIPE extracts and strengthens those signals without additional training. Its first component analyzes the joint embedding matrix of all frame prompts using singular-value decomposition. Adaptive rescaling strengthens components associated with identity and suppresses variation specific to individual frames. Its second component, Union Key, aligns the image generator’s image-text attention across the sequence. Together, these mechanisms address consistency through both prompt representations and how the image model attends to them.

On ConsiStory+, BIPE outperforms the evaluated existing methods in qualitative and quantitative comparisons. The authors also introduce DiverStory to evaluate a wider range of scenarios and prompt templates, providing further evidence of scalability. The contribution is a plug-and-play way to improve subject consistency by making greater use of identity information already present in text embeddings.
icml-2026-boost-the-identity-preserving-.tldr: BIPE improves subject consistency across generated images by extracting and strengthening identity signals already present in prompt embeddings.

paragraphs: Turning a written construction request into a viable structure requires language understanding, spatial reasoning, and compliance with physical constraints. BuildArena creates an interactive benchmark for assessing these capabilities together. It addresses a gap between language models’ broad reasoning abilities and the limited evaluation of their ability to perform engineering construction.

The benchmark contributes an extendable strategy for designing tasks across multiple difficulty levels. Those tasks cover both static and dynamic mechanics, bringing different physical requirements into the evaluation. A second contribution is a library for geometric computation in three-dimensional space, which supports construction from language instructions. Together, the task design and computation library provide infrastructure for studying language-driven construction under physical constraints.

The authors evaluate nine frontier language models and three additional open-weight models using this framework. The abstract establishes the scope of that evaluation without reporting a model ranking or numerical outcome. The paper’s stated contribution is therefore chiefly an evaluation resource: a way to examine integrated construction competence in an interactive, physics-grounded setting, with released code supporting further work.
icml-2026-buildarena-a-physics-aligned-i.tldr: BuildArena evaluates whether language models can turn written construction instructions into structures that satisfy physical requirements.

paragraphs: Additional context can make a language model less accurate when that context is irrelevant or harmful. This paper defines a concrete reference for protection: the model’s performance without any supplied context. Here, “safe” refers to that zero-shot performance baseline, giving the method a measurable target for limiting context-induced degradation.

The approach combines distribution-free risk control with dynamic early exiting. It avoids later attention heads that attend most strongly to unsafe inputs, limiting how much those inputs influence the prediction. The authors also modify the risk-control procedure so that protection against harmful context can coexist with benefits from useful context. This matters because a system that simply ignores every input would lose the advantages of contextual information.

The paper presents theoretical and empirical results across nine tasks covering in-context learning and open-ended question answering. Those results show effective control of performance risk from harmful context, alongside substantial computational savings when context is helpful. The contribution connects statistical control of degradation with a mechanism that can also reduce inference work.
icml-2026-controlling-the-risk-of-corrup.tldr: The method combines risk control and early exiting to limit damage from harmful context while retaining efficiency gains from helpful inputs.

paragraphs: A model trained on several tasks shares internal representations, but that sharing can also let tasks interfere with one another. CORE-MTL argues that adjusting gradient magnitudes or changing shared architecture leaves an underlying problem unresolved: shared features can mix useful task information with incidental context. This mixture can harm transfer and performance on unfamiliar data.

The proposed framework separates the representation into semantic and residual streams. The semantic stream concentrates information relevant to the tasks, while the residual stream carries nuisance variation. For visual tasks, the authors implement this separation using physical priors for structured scenes and statistical constraints for attributes. The approach changes what information is shared, making representation content central to how tasks interact during learning.

The theoretical analysis gives a tighter out-of-distribution generalization bound than optimization-centered methods and shows reduced gradient interference without explicit gradient projection or reweighting. On visual multi-task benchmarks, CORE-MTL consistently improves over the compared methods both within and outside the training distribution. These findings support separating useful structure from context as a route to more effective task sharing.
icml-2026-core-mtl-rethinking-gradient-b.tldr: CORE-MTL separates task-relevant features from nuisance variation to reduce interference and improve visual multi-task generalization.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses a training dataset into a small synthetic substitute. A difficulty is that the substitute can encode patterns tailored to the architecture used during distillation, reducing its usefulness for other models. DIVER addresses this problem through a second stage that recovers more transferable semantic information from distilled images.

The framework uses a pretrained diffusion model through three connected operations. Semantic inheritance moves high-level information from abstract distilled images into latent space, filtering architecture-specific noise. Semantic guidance directs the reverse generation process to preserve that information. Semantic fusion controls when this guidance is applied, restricting it to the concrete phase of the reverse process to avoid ambiguity and artifacts while retaining useful guidance.

Experiments show improvements to classical distillation techniques and substantial gains when distilled data is used across different architectures. The authors also report processing time comparable to raw DiT on ImageNet at 256-by-256 resolution, with 4 GB of GPU memory usage. The findings suggest that recovering semantics from existing distilled data can improve its portability without an especially large memory requirement in the reported setting.
icml-2026-diver-diving-deeper-into-disti.tldr: DIVER uses a pretrained diffusion model to recover transferable semantics from distilled datasets, improving their usefulness across architectures.

paragraphs: Neural operators work well on structured domains, but irregular geometry presents a less understood challenge. This paper argues that supplying a good geometric encoding at the input does not fully address the problem. Information about the domain’s shape can become progressively less accessible as it passes through deeper operator layers.

The authors formalize this behavior as the Geometric Forgetting Hypothesis, connecting it to the Markovian structure of operator layers and their use of global mixing. They probe geometry at successive layers and find declining geometric fidelity in both spectral and attention-based operators. Their analysis links this loss to worse accuracy, stability, and generalization, making retention through depth a central architectural concern.

To counter the loss, the paper introduces geometry memory injection, a lightweight mechanism that restores geometric constraints at intermediate layers. It consistently mitigates forgetting with little architectural overhead. The intervention also reveals a geometric-shortcut instability in transformer-based operators. Together, these findings motivate maintaining access to geometry throughout the model, beyond representing it well at the initial input.
icml-2026-do-neural-operators-forget-geo.tldr: The paper shows that neural operators lose geometric information with depth and proposes intermediate geometry injections to mitigate that loss.

paragraphs: Reinforcement fine-tuning teaches language-model agents through feedback from an environment. Evaluating them only in the environment where they trained leaves an important question open: whether the learned behavior transfers when knowledge requirements, observations, or available actions change. This paper systematically examines that generalization question.

The study separates three kinds of transfer. It tests changes in task difficulty within one environment, movement to previously unseen environments, and sequential training across multiple environments. The sequential setting also measures whether learning later environments erodes earlier abilities. This design distinguishes handling harder tasks under familiar conditions from adapting to a different setting with a different interface.

The results show good generalization across difficulty within an environment, but unstable transfer to unseen environments. That instability correlates with changes in semantic priors and observation or action interfaces. Sequential training produces promising gains on downstream environments with little forgetting of earlier ones, while training on mixtures improves the overall balance. The findings give a qualified picture: the benefits of reinforcement fine-tuning depend on the kind of shift being tested.
icml-2026-does-reinforcement-fine-tuning.tldr: Reinforcement fine-tuning transfers well across task difficulty in familiar environments, but transfer to unseen environments is less reliable.

paragraphs: Long-video diffusion transformers spend substantial inference time computing attention across space and time. Sparse attention saves work by removing some query-key interactions, but some attention heads remain too dense for that strategy to work well. EchoAttention targets an additional form of redundancy that remains available in those heads.

The authors observe that blocks of attention weights associated with frames often have similar distributions. Lightweight linear calibration can approximate these related blocks. EchoAttention combines a Sparse operator, which removes redundant token-pair interactions, with an Echo operator, which exploits similarity between frame blocks. A fine-grained routing policy learned through three-stage distillation chooses how to use these operations, enabling the system to handle both sparse and non-sparse heads.

Across public video diffusion transformers, the method consistently improves the reported speed-quality trade-off over leading sparse-attention baselines. It achieves end-to-end speedups of up to 2.42 times with minimal quality loss. The result shows why exploiting multiple kinds of attention redundancy can extend efficiency gains beyond what interaction pruning alone achieves in the evaluated models.
icml-2026-echoattention-exploiting-token.tldr: EchoAttention combines sparse attention with reuse of similar frame-level attention patterns, achieving up to 2.42-times faster video generation.

paragraphs: Counterfactual image generation asks how an image would change under a causal intervention. A useful result must reflect the intended intervention without introducing unrelated changes. The paper identifies a problem with standard classifier-free guidance: one global guidance scale controls all attributes, which can amplify changes that do not belong in the inferred counterfactual.

Factored Classifier-Free Guidance introduces separate control for attributes according to a causal graph. This gives the generation process more precise control over how guidance affects different properties. The method is model-agnostic and can also extend advanced guidance schemes, including CFG++ and APG. Its contribution is a flexible modification to guidance that incorporates causal structure into attribute-level control.

Experiments on natural and medical images show substantial improvements in how well generated counterfactuals satisfy the evaluated axiomatic requirements. The method reduces spurious amplification and improves reversibility of counterfactual changes. These findings concern consistency with counterfactual principles as well as generation behavior: a plausible-looking image is more useful for this task when its changes follow the intended causal intervention.
icml-2026-factored-classifier-free-guida.tldr: Factored Classifier-Free Guidance uses causal structure to control image attributes separately and reduce unintended counterfactual changes.

paragraphs: In self-supervised goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, agents often use previously observed states as goals without receiving external rewards. A fixed observation-based goal representation can be awkward: it may demand an exact visual match or leave distinct states ambiguous. This paper develops a goal space that includes both specific targets and broader concepts.

The method learns a latent space with a partial ordering using an energy function. Subset relations between observations organize goals into a hierarchy running from concrete to abstract. This structure allows the representation to distinguish particular states while also capturing concepts shared across them. The agent therefore has access to different levels of specificity within one learned goal space.

In navigation and robotic manipulation experiments, agents trained with this hierarchy achieve higher task success and better generalization to novel tasks than agents using purely observational goals. The findings support learning relationships among goals as part of the representation itself. Those relationships help connect the precision needed to identify a particular state with the abstraction useful for transferring behavior to new tasks.
icml-2026-hierarchical-goal-abstractions.tldr: Learning subset relations among goals gives reinforcement-learning agents a hierarchy that combines precise targets with transferable abstract concepts.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models rely on transformer decoders whose modules repeatedly update a shared representation through residual connections. This paper develops a framework using information theory and geometry to examine what those updates do. It seeks a common theoretical account of module behavior beyond statistical attribution alone.

The analysis finds a division of labor between attention and feed-forward networks. Attention primarily rearranges information while preserving its representational subspace. Feed-forward networks expand that subspace, contributing what the authors describe as semantic innovation. This distinction provides a way to examine whether computational effort in the architecture corresponds to meaningful changes in its representations.

The authors then replace learned attention weights with predefined alternatives, including Gaussian noise. Across a majority of the evaluated datasets, these replacements produce comparable or better performance than the original models. The result suggests substantial redundancy and misallocation in the examined attention mechanisms. Its scope is the reported models and evaluations: the evidence challenges how effectively their learned attention uses visual context, without establishing that attention is universally dispensable.
icml-2026-large-vision-language-models-g.tldr: A geometric and information-theoretic analysis finds attention redundancy in vision-language models, with predefined weights matching or improving many evaluated results.

paragraphs: Key-value caching saves language models from repeating earlier computations, but conventional caches incorporate token positions into their stored representations. That makes reuse difficult when the same retrieved content appears at different positions in different requests. Existing approaches either restrict where reuse is possible or incur costly memory operations to change positional encoding.

LazyAttention postpones positional encoding until the attention computation needs it. Specialized kernels adjust positions on the fly, allowing one physical cache copy to support several logical requests at arbitrary positions. This zero-copy design removes the need to materialize position-adjusted copies. The system provides kernels for both prefilling the context and decoding subsequent output.

Under skewed document distributions, LazyAttention reports a 1.37-times reduction in time to first token and 1.40-times higher throughput than Block-Attention, with comparable output quality. The workload condition matters to interpreting these gains because the method is designed to make cached content more reusable. Its central contribution is separating physical cache storage from the positions that content occupies in individual requests.
icml-2026-lazyattention-efficient-retrie.tldr: LazyAttention applies positional encoding inside attention kernels so requests can reuse one KV-cache copy at different positions without copying it.

paragraphs: Block-wise diffusion language models generate several tokens in parallel, but long-context attention can remain limited by memory access. Simply making each query sparse does not necessarily solve this problem. Different queries may select different prefix positions, so their combined requests still load a large collection of key-value memory pages.

LoSA uses an observation about successive denoising steps: only a small fraction of tokens undergo large changes in their hidden representations. It reuses cached prefix-attention results for stable tokens and computes sparse attention for active tokens with substantial changes. Fewer queries then contribute new key-value requests, shrinking the total set of pages that must be loaded.

Across several block-wise diffusion models and reasoning benchmarks, LoSA maintains accuracy close to dense attention while improving efficiency. The reported speedup reaches 4.14 times over dense attention on RTX A6000 GPUs. These findings show how temporal stability during denoising can make sparsity more effective at the memory-system level. The method reduces repeated attention work while directly addressing the combined memory footprint of active queries.
icml-2026-losa-locality-aware-sparse-att.tldr: LoSA reuses attention results for stable tokens and sparsifies changing tokens, reaching up to 4.14-times speedup with near-dense accuracy.

paragraphs: Medical language models need knowledge updates as information changes. Editing through retrieval offers a way to supply updated knowledge without full retraining, but similar medical concepts can overlap in representation space and cause the wrong update to be retrieved. The paper also identifies batch editing as an underexplored requirement for applying multiple updates.

The authors introduce MedVersa, an expanded benchmark covering both individual and batch edits across a broader medical knowledge range. It imposes strict locality requirements, meaning an edit should preserve behavior outside its intended scope. Their MedREK framework combines a shared query-key module for more precise retrieval matching with an attention-based prompt encoder that supplies informative guidance to the model.

Across the evaluated medical benchmarks, MedREK consistently improves the reported key metrics. The authors also report the first validated solution for batch editing in medical language models. The contribution links retrieval accuracy with controlled update scope: selecting the relevant edit and presenting it effectively are both central to making knowledge changes while preserving unrelated behavior.
icml-2026-medrek-retrieval-based-editing.tldr: MedREK improves retrieval-based medical knowledge editing through precise query-key matching and guided prompts, including support for batch edits.

paragraphs: Agent memory must grow without making relevant information difficult to retrieve. Abstracting information helps manage that growth, but can hide details needed for later reasoning. Memora proposes a memory representation that combines broad organization with access to specific stored values, addressing this tension within the structure of memory itself.

Its primary abstractions index concrete memory values and consolidate related updates into unified entries. Cue anchors provide additional ways to access a memory through its different aspects and connect it to related memories. A retrieval policy actively follows these connections, allowing retrieval to reach useful information beyond items that directly resemble the query in semantic space.

The authors theoretically show that standard retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge-graph memory systems arise as special cases of their framework. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, Memora achieves reported state-of-the-art results, with better retrieval relevance and reasoning effectiveness as memory scales. The findings support combining abstraction, preserved detail, and connected retrieval rather than relying on a single route from a query to a stored memory.
icml-2026-memora-a-harmonic-memory-repre.tldr: Memora organizes detailed memories under abstractions and connected retrieval cues to improve retrieval and reasoning as agent memory grows.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can generate effective robot actions while still violating physical constraints. PACT addresses safety after a policy has been pretrained. It adapts the policy toward feasible trajectories without accessing demonstration data or task rewards, making physical constraints the basis for this additional training stage.

The framework distills constraint gradients into the diffusion model using a reverse-KL objective, with supervision distributed across diffusion timesteps. A curriculum gradually tightens constraints rather than imposing their full strength immediately. The authors connect this progression to theoretical bounds on policy change and monotone improvement. Controlling how far the policy shifts is intended to reduce catastrophic forgetting and the resulting tension between safety and task performance.

On simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks, PACT reduces safety violations by 31.0% on average while improving task success by 30.7%. These reported results show that the evaluated safety alignment also benefits task completion. The contribution is a post-training mechanism that incorporates constraint information into the policy itself while managing disruption to its existing behavior.
icml-2026-pact-self-evolving-physical-sa.tldr: PACT post-trains diffusion robot policies using physical constraints, reducing violations while improving task success in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic table rows requires capturing relationships among numerical and categorical variables. Q-Tab explores code-based generation with a masked-language-model transformer. The paper identifies a difficulty with conventional codebooks: useful tabular generation needs a code space larger than the training sample, including codes that can support new rows.

Q-Tab jointly tokenizes numerical variables with lookup-free quantization and residual corruption, while categorical variables receive direct one-hot tokenization. A BERT-style masked model learns dependencies among these tokens and supports sampling. Corruption spreads reconstruction supervision across the numerical code space, helping train codes beyond those directly represented by the original examples.

That broader supervision introduces a complication: when encoder and decoder learn together, reconstruction targets move, and the corruption structure affects how difficult this regression becomes. Residual quantization balances coverage with locality to address this issue. The authors report state-of-the-art predictive utility and label prediction while matching diffusion generators in distributional fidelity. These results indicate that the token-based approach can produce useful synthetic tables while preserving their statistical resemblance to the data.
icml-2026-q-tab-quantized-tabular-data-g.tldr: Q-Tab combines residual lookup-free quantization with masked token modeling to generate statistically faithful and predictively useful synthetic tables.

paragraphs: Autoregressive video generators retain key-value caches that grow with the generated history and can dominate GPU memory. This creates both a deployment problem and a quality problem. Restricting the available history limits working memory, which can weaken consistency in subject identity, scene layout, and motion over long videos.

Quant VideoGen is a training-free framework for compressing that cache. Semantic-Aware Smoothing exploits similarities across space and time to produce small residual values that are easier to quantize. Progressive Residual Quantization then represents those residuals through multiple coarse-to-fine stages. This combination reduces quantization error while providing a gradual trade-off between memory consumption and generation quality.

Across LongCat-Video, HY-WorldPlay, and Self-Forcing, the framework improves the reported quality-memory frontier. It reduces key-value memory by up to seven times with less than 4% added end-to-end latency and substantially better generation quality than the evaluated baselines. The findings make cache compression relevant beyond fitting a model onto hardware: managing the cost of retained history also matters for coherent long-video generation.
icml-2026-quant-videogen-auto-regressive.tldr: Quant VideoGen compresses video-generation KV caches without training, reducing memory by up to seven times with less than 4% latency overhead.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification builds a class representation from very few labeled examples. A single noisy example can therefore pull the class prototype away from its useful location and damage generalization. This paper addresses that vulnerability using the geometry of examples in semantic feature space, where the authors find that clean samples occupy low-rank subspaces.

Noisy samples disrupt this structure through rank anomalies. The proposed method uses a differentiable low-rank approximation to estimate the support set’s intrinsic rank and identify anomalous examples. It then runs a rank-guided diffusion process to generate replacements under low-rank constraints. Detection and correction therefore use the same structural signal to reconstruct a more consistent support set.

On MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and other noisy benchmarks, the approach reduces prototype drift and significantly lowers errors at tested noise levels up to 40%. These findings support low-rank geometry as a useful signal when there are too few examples to rely on large-scale statistics. The contribution extends beyond identifying problematic samples by generating replacements intended to restore the support set’s class structure.
icml-2026-rank-guided-diffusion-for-nois.tldr: The method detects noisy few-shot examples through rank anomalies and uses constrained diffusion to replace them with more consistent samples.

paragraphs: Process reward models assess intermediate reasoning, providing learning signals before a final answer is available. Existing ways to train them can require strong information about expert policies or suffer problems such as entropy collapse. rePIRL seeks to learn useful process rewards while making minimal assumptions about the expert policies involved.

The framework draws on inverse reinforcement learning and alternates updates to the reasoning policy and the process reward model. It includes techniques tailored to the challenge of scaling inverse reinforcement learning to language models. The theoretical analysis places online and offline process-reward learning within one framework, supporting the claim that this approach can operate with reduced assumptions about experts.

Evaluations on standardized mathematical and coding reasoning datasets show improvements over the compared methods. The authors also demonstrate uses of the learned reward model in test-time training, test-time scaling, and early feedback during training on difficult problems. Ablation studies examine the training recipe and design choices. Together, these results position rePIRL as a framework for learning intermediate feedback that can support several stages of reasoning-model development and use.
icml-2026-repirl-learn-prm-with-inverse-.tldr: rePIRL alternately trains a reasoning policy and process reward model through an inverse-RL-inspired framework requiring minimal assumptions about experts.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation reduces the cost of fine-tuning language models, but fixed ranks constrain how much adaptation each layer can express. Dynamic alternatives can introduce substantial memory costs. Spectral Bridge Variational Inference develops a geometric approach that lets the effective rank change during learning while seeking computational efficiency.

The framework expresses LoRA as a continuous Wasserstein gradient flow over Gaussian distributions. A stochastic differential equation governs singular values through competition between task gradients and adaptive entropic friction. This mechanism suppresses noise-associated modes and strengthens components carrying useful signal, allowing rank allocation to emerge separately for each layer. The authors derive a linear-complexity algorithm using factorized Riemannian retractions and Empirical Bayes updates for friction.

On reasoning and coding benchmarks, SBVI achieves reported state-of-the-art performance with better accuracy and memory efficiency than the evaluated static and dynamic methods. The approach matters because adaptation capacity becomes something shaped by training signals rather than fully fixed at initialization. Its mathematical construction is paired with an algorithm intended to make that flexibility practical without the memory overhead of existing dynamic approaches.
icml-2026-spectral-bridge-variational-in.tldr: SBVI dynamically adjusts LoRA’s layer-wise ranks through geometric flows, improving reported accuracy and memory efficiency on reasoning and coding benchmarks.

paragraphs: Editing one part of a 3D object requires preserving its remaining structure and keeping the change consistent across viewpoints. Existing methods can be slow, distort geometry, or require carefully prepared 3D masks. This paper addresses both the training-data requirements and the model design needed for more controlled editing.

The authors introduce 3DEditVerse with 116,309 training pairs and 1,500 curated test pairs. Complementary pipelines produce pose-driven geometric changes and foundation-model-guided appearance changes, with locality, multi-view consistency, and semantic alignment. Their model, 3DEditFormer, builds on image-to-3D generation using dual-guidance attention and time-adaptive gating to separate regions that should change from structure that should remain.

The resulting system performs edits without auxiliary 3D masks. Experiments show quantitative and qualitative improvements over the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. The combined contribution is significant because consistent editing needs both suitable examples of localized changes and a model that can preserve surrounding structure. The dataset supplies paired supervision at scale, while the architecture explicitly manages the distinction between editable content and preserved geometry.
icml-2026-towards-scalable-and-consisten.tldr: 3DEditVerse and 3DEditFormer combine large-scale paired data with a structure-preserving model for consistent 3D edits without auxiliary masks.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can answer a video question using an initial interpretation that reflects its own biases. Video-BCI makes those interpretations explicit by first sampling several self-prior hypotheses. It then guides the model to critically integrate them, treating video reasoning as a Bayesian cognitive process that can challenge its initial consensus.

A composite utility function supplies two learning signals. The Dialectical Uncertainty Signal considers disagreement among hypotheses and rewards correct judgments that challenge the majority. The Process Tracing Signal directs learning toward reasoning paths within the model’s own hypotheses that produce better answers. Together, they encourage scrutiny of conflicting interpretations and extraction of useful reasoning procedures from the model’s existing proposals.

Across six mainstream video-understanding benchmarks, Video-BCI achieves reported state-of-the-art results, including a 3.8% improvement over the previous best on MMVU. The findings support using multiple internal hypotheses as material for critical reasoning. The mechanism goes beyond counting agreement by considering when a majority interpretation is wrong and which reasoning paths lead toward better answers.
icml-2026-video-bci-bayesian-cognitive-i.tldr: Video-BCI improves video reasoning by critically combining the model’s own hypotheses and learning from reasoning paths that yield better answers.
